rationale: Jev beats Laya on 9/11 decision points (76.7% vs 63.1% on A-F) but both fail zero-shot routing (Jev answers cheap 99.5%), tie on RAG (61.0 vs 60.5) and are unusable PII gates (Jev FPR 63-66%); vs the DeepSeek reference Jev is similar on tool selection (99.5 vs 98.5) but worse on embedded-injection TPR (90.8-93.3 vs 97.5-98.3) and PII FPR (63 vs 12) (Sec. 5, Tables 3,5,6,7).

Reversing option order changes 1.8% of Jev decisions but 30.3% of Laya's (53% with 60-77 labels), and instruction rewording moves accuracy 5-15 pp for both systems (Sec. 5 RQ2, Fig. 3); no generative comparator on these perturbations.

Pooled ECE 0.143 (Jev) vs 0.158 (Laya) on A-F and 0.080 vs 0.198 on G-J, Jev confidently constant on routing (ECE 0.477), 26% of Laya answers at conf>=0.9 wrong; per-domain Platt recalibration needed (Laya ECE 0.22->0.027) (Sec. 5 Calibration).

Jev pre-screen before an LLM reviewer keeps the in-sample miss rate (11.6% vs 11.6% LLM-only) but cuts cost only 4.3% at tau=0.1, adds an extra miss in 47% of held-out threshold splits, and 5% FNR targets are exceeded in about half of splits (p95 10-17%); Laya must pass 99.3%; Laya->Jev cascade lowers accuracy 76.7->70.7 (Sec. 6, Table 8).

Under random option permutation cross-head models (incl. Laya-large) change 10-17% of answers (S-PubMedBERT C: 3% seen, 17% held-out, 28% exams) while prior-fused/bi-encoder heads are essentially invariant (0.3%/0.0%) (Sec. 6.2, App. H Table 12); LLMs not tested for order.

After temperature scaling (an added step) seen-task ECE is 3.6-4.4 for all objectives vs 8.5-9.1 for zero-shot Gemma-4-31B/Qwen3.8-27B, but held-out tasks are poorly calibrated and long-note answerability stays near chance (Sec. 6.3-6.4, Table 2, Limitations, App. H).

Routing the 20% least-confident questions to Gemma raises macro accuracy 59.5->68.4 (S-PubMedBERT C) and 64.3->69.1 (Laya-large) vs 62.1 for Gemma alone, but this is a retrospective fixed budget on the test set with temperature-scaled confidence, not a validated threshold (Sec. 6.4, Fig. 3).

In-distribution SecJev reaches 94.51% task-macro (4B) vs 94.35% for matched generative SFT (similar), but on new sources it beats generation on BIPIA (72.00 vs 54.33) and trails on IoT-23 (65.10 vs 68.10, FPR 66.4% vs 51.4%), and VeReMi stays <72% (Tables 3-5, Sec. 5.2-5.4).

Paraphrasing changes accuracy by 0.07-0.93 pp and choice permutation by -0.80 to +0.40 pp, with answer agreement 95.36-98.36% (paraphrase) and 97.40-98.80% (permutation) across sizes, though 9B VeReMi agreement is 77% (Table 6, Sec. 6.1).

Security-test ECE is 1.53-2.18% raw and 2.48-3.56% after temperature scaling with Brier 0.173-0.213 across sizes; confidence on general suites is not fully recovered after specialization (Table 9, Sec. 6.3).

Matched controls (20 texts/task): neutral identifiers cut Qwen detection 20.0-30.6 pp while Jev changes are small (e.g. -4.0 order on DBpedia, -11.0 IDs on TREC), but task-aligned NONE wording raises Laya Emotion detection 25.0 pp and IDs raise Laya false rejection 12.5 pp (Sec. 3.4, Table 6).

Native abstention at k=5: Jev D/F 63.7%/3.3% vs Qwen 45.0%/3.7% (Laya 86.0%/27.7%), but transferred none-thresholds exceed 5% false rejection in 6/12 transfers (Jev DBpedia->Emotion F=69.3%; Emotion threshold disables detection) and work only with target-label recalibration (Sec. 3.1-3.2, Table 2).

Rejection/escalation thresholds calibrated on 80 source pairs fail to preserve the operating point on other tasks (6/12 transfers >5% false rejection for each of Laya and Jev; D/F 0/0 when Jev's Emotion threshold is 1.00), restored only by target recalibration (82.5%/3.3%) (Sec. 3.1, Fig. 2, Table 7).

Hosted Jev reaches ROC-AUC 0.95-1.0 on 8 detection benchmarks with calibrated accuracy 87-99% on security tasks, but AI-text detection needs a calibrated threshold (78%->89%) and NanoJev is near or below AUROC 0.5 on injection, jailbreak and AI-text (Sec. V-B, Fig. 8).

Content in the state steers decisions: Jev-specific injection and a universal suffix reach 97-100% ASR on Jev across Choice/Noul/Score (context ignoring 96.5-100% on two tasks), NanoJev 62-100%, and 5-10% poisoning backdoors NanoJev at 76-100% ASR (Tables I-II).

Typed outputs leak at scale: label-only attribute inference on hosted Jev reaches 100% coverage and accuracy for gender, age, heart disease and ethnicity, private facts that GPT-6 refused were inferred by interval queries, Jev-guided jailbreak refinement succeeds on 100/100 queries and extraction reaches 92% agreement (Tables IV-V, App. C).

Jev escalates when coverage is absent for 45/48 contract cases (DeepSeek 3/48, Gemini 14/48) but for only 4/120 infeasible routes (DeepSeek 67/120, GLM 109/120), and handles resolved observation conflicts in 11/120 (Sec. VII-C, Tables X-XI).

Engine-owned checks are unreliable (passes one coverage check, fails another; 11/120 resolved conflicts), while moving checks into an auditable controller workflow raises Jev correctness 29/120->84/120 (+45.8 pp, CI 37.5-54.2) and full rules satisfy all conditions; only 4/50 loop claims in the 139-family audit have matched evidence (Sec. V, VII-C, VIII).

The open Turkish model ranks 7th/16 on HakemBench (composite 0.660), decision quality 0.705 vs 0.741-0.901 for Qwen3.5-4B, DeepSeek, GLM, GPT and Gemini (Jev 1.13: 0.851), passes only 128/201 harmless guardrail look-alikes and scores below a surface-cue baseline on human-checked support (0.476 vs 0.619) (Table 2, Sec. 6).

Order sensitivity is 0.000 by construction (bit-for-bit permutation test) vs 0.039 (Jev) to 0.590 (Laya) among other board models; paraphrase agreement 0.883 vs Jev 0.926 with overlapping intervals; a sequential head changed 2.3-2.8% of answers under reordering (Sec. 1, 6, Table 4).

Temperature scaling raised held-out ECE 0.027->0.045 (Run 1), the not-sure signal misses guardrail errors (12.2% wrong among 148 guardrail answers at conf>=0.99), guardrail smooth ECE 0.158, and calibration axis 0.482 is below Gemini/GPT/GLM (0.706-0.806) but above DeepSeek (0.386) (Sec. 5, Table 2).

Under seven fixed candidate orders, node-local Shared-KV correct Acquire decisions range 90-113/120 (global 14-90/120) and order changes the selected value in 46/120 node-local and 120/120 global states (Sec. IV-B).

With an explicit ABSTAIN candidate Shared-KV rejects 28/30 invalid cases but gets only 17/30 valid ones right (45/60 vs 51/60 for autoregressive generation); authors conclude candidate scores cannot be treated as confidence (Sec. IV-F).

Decomposing decisions into node-local typed fields raises correct joint decisions to 113/120 vs 90/120 global and 68/120 constrained AR and makes failures attributable, but correct progression relies on external postconditions: without them model completion ends 10/15 states prematurely (Sec. IV-B, IV-C, IV-G).

Confidence-based deferral is unreliable (ABSTAIN 45/60 vs AR 51/60) while external postcondition gates block 7/8 premature completion requests and the recovery branch fires in 10/10 injected failures (restoring progress in 1) (Sec. IV-E to IV-G).

ECE falls from 0.105 to 0.082 at loop 3 then rises to 0.093 at loop 8 (Qwen3.5-4B typed 0.113); evidence AUROC 0.935 with hard answers on evidence-removed items 27.1%->17.5%, but confidence rises on wrong answers (0.567->0.660), 19.7% of errors carry conf>=0.9, and averaging loops is needed to halve ECE to 0.044 (Sec. 5.3, Table 2).

On 190 natural traces Jev source-support has AUROC 0.986 and Brier 0.034 and withholds all 27 unsupported-role traces at 0.8, but on same-number swaps 4 of 6 wrong-role citations stay accepted and on 36 fresh pages only 8/15 A-only-supported pairs are separated (Sec. III-A, III-B, III-D).

Repeating the column header (same information) flips all 8 wrong-role B calls from accepted to withheld (interactions -0.34 to -0.83) but also lowers support for equivalent facts (2 of 6 equivalent B means already <0.8; fresh-source supported-A withholding 5->6) (Sec. III-B to III-D, Figs. 1-3).

Jev alone matches 95/96 keys; the <0.8 gate escalated 12 questions that were already correct and fallback to GPT-4.1-mini traces lowered matches by 1.56 pp (CI -4.17 to 0), while the sole Jev error had p=0.8 and escaped the strict gate (Sec. IV, Table III).

Direct Jev averages 62.93% macro-F1 on 8 affect datasets, above 5 of 10 LLM configurations but below Gemini IO (67.28%) and far below on HD humor (61.80 vs 87.92); ranks first on no dataset (Sec. 4.3, Table 2).

Decomposing classification into atomic Jev judgments (Emo-Jev-D) yields 62.00% vs 62.93% direct macro-F1, improving only CMMA and falling on 7 datasets; it stays below the best generative configuration (67.28%) (Sec. 4.3, Table 2).

Task-trained typed verifier reaches 96.15% accuracy/96.04% BA (untuned 82.05%), but human-preference agreement 63.49% vs 60.32% for direct Qwen3.5-27B scoring has CI -8.33 to 16.67 and top-candidate identity risk is not reduced (47.62 vs 45.24) (Tables 2-3).

Atomic per-question probabilities are retained for inspection and expose identity/relation failures a holistic score hides (post-hoc case CP_Object_030), but the mean can compensate failed critical conditions and agreement gains over holistic 27B scoring are not significant (Sec. 3.5, 5.3, Fig. 3).

On SDDBench, Chip ECE 0.0032/Brier 0.0551 and hosted Jev ECE 0.0271 vs 0.0307-0.0607 for Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol and DeepSeek; out of domain on JevBench Chip ECE rises to 0.1633 (Original) and 0.3577 (Hard) (Tables 3-4).
Per-request latency 118 ms (Chip) and 1,510 ms (Jev) vs 4,631-16,009 ms for flagship LLMs and 18.4-25.3 s for small LLMs, with Chip valid on all 5,000 records (Jev 678 failures) (Tables 3, 6).

Jev-read narratives yield statewide counts over 5,018,080 Texas crashes that a second human tier confirms for all 15 estimates, but only after human recalibration; flags were confirmed about 1 in 7 for unbelted vs about 9 in 10 for phone use and fatigue, and a Kumo-ranked re-read list gives 7-58x lift (Abstract, Sec. 4.1, 6).

The identity (uncalibrated) map was ineligible for every factor except vehicle defects because Jev probabilities overstate the human rate; Platt/isotonic recalibration with a coded-field shift eta=2.00 (0.37-4.50) was required (App. B, Table B.2).

Population-scale use is feasible (reading every narrative costs about 773 USD; 5.6M crashes) but validity rests on a human tier: recalibration uncertainty dominates and 400 more human-coded narratives cut RMS relative half-width 22.0%->16.2% vs 21.2% for reading every narrative (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 8).
